source.title: Asymmetric Capacity Allocation in Self-Refinement Pipelines
source.authors: Zhuo-Yi Yang; Ian G. Harris; Salar Hashemitaheri; Cassie Huang; Yuan-Gang Li; Hyunwoo Oh; Paul Dourish; T. Givargis; Mohsen Imani; Li Zhang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It examines model-size effects in a new setting—multi-stage self-refinement—and reports downstream benchmark results. It does not measure pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream task-score sweeps and sensitivity summaries for self-refinement stages, so these bear on V6 in this new setting. It does not report held-out pretraining loss or test V1–V5 or V7. The scaling-law discussion in Related Works is background and citations, not results from this study. Table 3's critique-versus-no-critique gains are not model-size sweep results and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background in Related Works. Its results are stage-wise sensitivity summaries (range ∆ and across-size std) for off-the-shelf Qwen3 and Gemma 3 models placed in a generate–critique–refine pipeline, plus counts of refiner sizes that fall below the initial generation. None of this measures pretraining loss, fits a law, or tests whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. ∆ and Std are sensitivity scores and do not show direction. The claim that larger generators help rests on figure curves and prose, with no predictive relation fitted. The question asked is about allocating capacity across pipeline stages, a related but different construct. The record's V6 link is therefore dropped, and the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find that generator and refiner capacity strongly affect self-refinement performance and critic size matters little. Even a 0.6B critic beats no critique, a weak refiner can hurt initial performance, and capacity should be allocated non-uniformly. They do not claim anything about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study performs inference-time stage-wise model-size sweeps on self-refinement pipelines and measures benchmark task scores. It does not use the original sources' pretraining-loss scaling-law fits or training-compute allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with pipeline stage and model family/configuration. The study also evaluates different benchmarks; it reports that qualitative stage-wise trends are consistent across Qwen3 and Gemma 3 and across Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-8B configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: In self-refinement pipelines, performance is far more sensitive to generator and refiner size than to critic size. Examples: Qwen3 PIE std 10.43 (generator), 20.60 (refiner), 1.63 (critic). The same pattern holds in Gemma 3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multi-stage inference pipelines, returns to model size differ by stage. Critic capacity matters least.

fits_no_version.finding: Undersized refiners can make output worse than the initial generation. Counts: 12/30 (Qwen3-32B config), 9/30 (14B), 8/30 (8B), 8/20 (Gemma 27B). Mostly the refiner alters correct content.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small refiner models in self-refinement can degrade correct initial solutions.

record.problems: The results cover five benchmark subsets, two model families, and one refinement iteration; the authors note that findings may not generalize to more complex agentic systems, additional architectures, tasks, or modalities. Main paper Table 1 reports ranges and standard deviations across model sizes rather than all per-size scores; score curves are presented in figures. These are downstream pipeline outcomes, not pretraining-loss scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible reported results were left out. The 30 Table 1 stage-by-benchmark summaries are retained, along with all four Table 4 aggregate degradation counts and the separate manual degradation analysis. Table 3's critique-gain comparison is excluded because it compares critique with no critique rather than testing model-size scaling.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No architecture-shape variation at fixed size.
No other modalities and no training regimes such as fine-tuning or repeated data.
No predictive relation between scale or loss and downstream score is fitted or tested. Sizes are pipeline-stage choices of off-the-shelf models.
No exponents and no fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the study to V6 because downstream scores vary with model size. However, the swept quantity is the size of one pipeline stage, and the summary statistics (range/std) carry no direction. Nothing tests whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss. Per-size scores exist only in Figures 4 and 7–9 and are not tabulated. Even read from the figures, they would show monotone improvement for the generator, not a predictive law. Table 3 (critique gains) is correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy or loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions of larger-run loss are made.
No fixed training-compute budget, parameter/token allocation, or compute-optimal split is studied.
The study varies model size, not architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test the same power-law form across modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests downstream benchmark outcomes against the size of individual stages in a self-refinement pipeline; it does not test prediction from pretraining loss, extrapolation from smaller runs, or a quantitative predictive law.
It does not compare scaling-law exponents or fitting choices, or test whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Qwen3-32B configuration
rows.size_stated: 0.6B refiner compared with 32B refiner
rows.operation_detail: Manually analyzed 50 degradation events from P(32B,32B,0.6B), comparing outputs against initial generation and the 32B refiner under the same initial solution and critique.

conditions.value: 0.6B and 32B refiner outputs under the same initial solution and critique

rows.measure: Manual characterization of degradation events
rows.value: In all 50 events, the 0.6B refiner produced a worse output than both the initial generation and the 32B refiner; 41 events had non-misleading critiques (scores 3–5), and 9 had misleading critiques (scores 1–2).
rows.uncertainty: 50 manually analyzed events; no additional uncertainty reported
rows.note: Authors attribute the common failure to the 0.6B refiner changing correct content; in 9 cases it followed misleading feedback.
rows.check: Qualitative failure analysis of 50 events with a 0.6B refiner. This is error characterisation, not a scaling result.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Generator and refiner sweeps across the tested benchmarks and configurations
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that generator scaling consistently improves end-to-end pipeline performance and that generator/refiner size has substantial effects; the benchmark-wise sensitivity summaries are in T1-Q-* and T1-G-* rows.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Critic-size changes are reported as marginal, and weak refiners sometimes fall below initial generation, including 12/30 Qwen3-32B cases and the analyzed Qwen3-0.6B-refiner events; thus downstream scaling depends on pipeline stage and allocation.
